Alright, let me think this through as I plan the year.

---

**My reasoning:**

I've been doing this 25 years now, so I know my land pretty well. 232.9 mu is a lot of ground for just three of us at home — me, my wife, and our kid — so I can't pretend I'll do this all myself. I hire help for the busy times: wheat harvest, maize planting, and the cauliflower work. That eats into profit, but there's no way around it.

My main system is wheat-maize double cropping, same as most folks around here. I run about 200 mu of the land in that rotation — it's the steady earner, and with the well I can irrigate when I need to. The rest, about 33 mu on the plot with better soil and closer to the road, I put in cauliflower. Cauliflower is more work and more risk, but the price is better than grain, and I've been doing it for years so I know the buyers.

**Wheat** (planted last October, managing through June now): I put down a compound fertilizer before planting — around 40 kg/mu of the 15-15-15 stuff — and I'll topdress urea at green-up and again at jointing if the crop looks like it needs it. Altogether about 18 kg of N per mu, that's what the extension guy recommended and it matches what I've been doing. I'll irrigate three times: green-up in early March, jointing in April, and filling in May. Last year I got about 470 kg/mu. Weather looks okay so far, so I'm hoping for similar.

**Maize** (goes in right after wheat harvest in mid-June): Tight turnaround — I pay the custom operator to come in with the no-till planter because I don't have time to plow. Hybrid seed, about 50 yuan/mu. I usually put 15-16 kg N/mu, some at planting and topdress at the big-trumpet stage. Usually irrigate once or twice depending on summer rain. Good year I get 520, bad year 400.

**Cauliflower** (33 mu, more intensive): Spring crop transplants go in mid-March, harvest late May-June. Then I can do a second autumn crop on the same ground — transplant in August, harvest November. This crop needs more fertilizer and more water, so I budget around 25 kg N/mu, plus manure if I can get it cheap. More pesticide too — cabbage worms and diamondback moths are a constant headache. It costs a lot to grow but the price per mu is three or four times what grain pays, when the market holds.

I don't try to push the limits on inputs. I apply about what I did last year because I know it works. If I under-apply and lose yield, that's a much bigger hit than spending a bit extra on fertilizer I don't strictly need.
